chunks.title: EcoStruxure FlexReady API · Energy Interactive Product — page intro
chunks.text: Energy Interactive Without Limits A centralized, extensible integration layer that standardizes how Schneider Electric's internal systems interact with external flexibility actors — DSOs, aggregators, and energy markets — so every Line of Business can deliver flexibility services without redesigning their core products. Key stats: 5 Key Capabilities; 1 Integration Layer; IEC 62746-4 Standard Aligned; All LOBs Supported

chunks.title: Section: Product overview
chunks.text: Product overview: With the increasing demand for energy flexibility and integration with external entities such as DSOs, aggregators, and energy markets, it is essential that all Lines of Business across our organization are equipped to interact in a consistent, secure, and scalable way. Historically, each LOB has developed its own products and platforms to manage customer sites for energy monitoring, control, and reporting.

chunks.title: Section: Purpose of the product
chunks.text: Purpose of the product: The Energy Interactive Product is a centralized, extensible integration layer that standardizes how our internal systems interact with external flexibility actors. It provides:

chunks.title: Section: Vision
chunks.text: Vision: Our goal is to empower each LOB to deliver flexibility capabilities to their customers without having to redesign their core products. Instead, by integrating with the Energy Interactive Product, LOBs can:

chunks.title: Section: Key capabilities
chunks.text: Key capabilities: The Energy Interactive Product is designed to serve as a unified integration and intelligence layer across the organization, enabling seamless delivery of flexibility services. It provides a set of foundational capabilities that LOBs can adopt incrementally, prioritized based on MVP focus and long-term vision.

chunks.title: MARKET / OPPORTUNITY — page intro
chunks.text: Energy complexity at scale From retail to public infrastructure, Energy Interactive serves organizations facing the same reality: managing energy flexibility across large, fragmented portfolios. This page frames the market context and the segments where the opportunity is strongest. Key stats: 5 Target segments; Scale Multi-site focus; B2B Organisationnel

chunks.title: Market situation
chunks.text: Market situation: The energy market is facing growing complexity: price volatility, increasing regulatory pressure (flexibility targets, decarbonization), and highly uneven digital maturity across players. Demand for flexibility services is surging, driven by electrification and the integration of intermittent renewable energy.

chunks.title: Trends & constraints
chunks.text: Trends & constraints: Structural trends: site digitalization, ESG requirements, the shift to real time, and data-driven decisions. Major constraints: integration costs, a shifting regulatory framework, legacy systems (heterogeneous EMS/BMS), and data silos between business lines and external players.

chunks.title: Customer problems to solve
chunks.text: Customer problems to solve: Difficulty leveraging site data, lack of interactivity with market players (DSOs, aggregators), slow decisions due to the absence of real-time tools, and low adoption of existing solutions seen as too complex or too vertical.

chunks.title: Section: Market situation
chunks.text: Market situation: Framing and legitimizing the market opportunity — a macro, factual and neutral view, with no reference to the offer.

chunks.title: Section: Target segments in the flexibility market
chunks.text: Target segments in the flexibility market: Five families of organizations share the same reality — energy complexity at portfolio scale. These are organizational-level players (not personas), managing multiple sites with flexibility potential that is still largely untapped.

chunks.title: MARKET TRENDS — page intro
chunks.text: The forces reshaping energy flexibility Three structural trends are driving the demand for flexibility services — and define why a unified, standardized integration layer like FlexReady matters now. Key stats: 3 Structural trends; DERs At the edge; AI Real-time enabler

chunks.title: Trend theme: Key drivers of flexibility demand
chunks.text: Key drivers of flexibility demand: The structural forces pushing electricity systems toward greater flexibility — on both the supply and demand sides.

chunks.title: Key drivers of flexibility demand — Renewable energy expansion
chunks.text: Renewable energy expansion: Rapid growth in wind and solar increases variability in the power system, driving the need for flexible resources that can balance intermittent generation.

chunks.title: Key drivers of flexibility demand — Flexibility services & storage
chunks.text: Flexibility services & storage: Cost reductions, better performance and supportive policies are accelerating battery storage. Batteries deliver fast-response services like frequency regulation and balancing for grid stability.

chunks.title: Key drivers of flexibility demand — Electrification of end-use sectors
chunks.text: Electrification of end-use sectors: Electric vehicles, heat pumps and industrial electrification raise overall electricity demand and create new load patterns the grid must absorb.

chunks.title: Trend theme: Decentralisation & prosumers
chunks.text: Decentralisation & prosumers: Energy generation and consumption are moving to the edge of the grid, turning consumers into active participants.

chunks.title: Decentralisation & prosumers — Rise of distributed energy resources
chunks.text: Rise of distributed energy resources: Growing use of rooftop solar, EVs and smart systems is decentralising both energy generation and consumption across the network.

chunks.title: Decentralisation & prosumers — Prosumers & flexibility
chunks.text: Prosumers & flexibility: Consumers become prosumers — producing and consuming energy. This increases available flexibility but also adds system complexity.

chunks.title: Decentralisation & prosumers — Aggregation & energy communities
chunks.text: Aggregation & energy communities: Aggregation combines small, scattered assets into market-ready portfolios, while energy communities enable local flexibility and citizen participation.

chunks.title: Decentralisation & prosumers — Challenges & policy considerations
chunks.text: Challenges & policy considerations: Data management, cybersecurity and equitable market access are key challenges that require active, ongoing policy development.

chunks.title: Trend theme: Digitalisation & AI
chunks.text: Digitalisation & AI: Technology is the enabler that makes flexibility operational at scale, in real time.

chunks.title: Digitalisation & AI — Enabling energy flexibility
chunks.text: Enabling energy flexibility: Digitalisation integrates smart meters and automated controls, enabling responsive and efficient energy flexibility markets.

chunks.title: Digitalisation & AI — AI for forecasting & optimization
chunks.text: AI for forecasting & optimization: AI and machine learning forecast demand, optimize dispatch and manage distributed energy resources more effectively than manual methods.

chunks.title: Digitalisation & AI — Automation & decentralization
chunks.text: Automation & decentralization: As flexibility decentralises, automation becomes essential — the system requires fast, real-time response that goes beyond manual control.

This is the pitch: minimal operational burden, SE and the EMS maintainer carry the heavy lifting.

chunks.title: Section: How the aggregator activates a support request
chunks.text: How the aggregator activates a support request: The aggregator submits an issue ticket through the Developer Portal Support Hub for recurring issues, bugs, or incidents. L1 support is the single point of contact, operated 24/7. It receives, processes and routes both aggregator-reported incidents and anomalies identified internally through proactive monitoring.

chunks.title: Section: How the aggregator is informed of platform changes

Breaking changes — any modification that would prevent an existing integration from functioning without changes — are only introduced through new API versions, with the previous version kept operational during the transition.

chunks.title: GLOSSARY — page intro
chunks.text: Speaking the same language A shared reference for the technical and commercial vocabulary of the FlexReady API — so operators, sales and partners align on the same terms. Type to filter across all sections.

chunks.title: Glossary: API (Application Programming Interface)
chunks.text: API (Application Programming Interface) (Technical): A standardized contract that lets two software systems exchange data. The FlexReady API is how external partners read from and write to the Energy Interactive platform.

chunks.title: Glossary: Northbound API
chunks.text: Northbound API (Technical): The outward-facing APIs that external stakeholders (DSOs, aggregators, markets) call to interact with the platform — as opposed to internal, system-facing integrations.

chunks.title: Glossary: REST
chunks.text: REST (Technical): An architectural style for web APIs based on standard HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT). The FlexReady API is RESTful and exchanges data in JSON.

chunks.title: Glossary: OAuth 2.0
chunks.text: OAuth 2.0 (Technical): The authorization standard used to secure API access: a partner obtains a token that grants scoped, time-limited permissions instead of sharing credentials.

chunks.title: Glossary: Telemetry
chunks.text: Telemetry (Technical): Real-time measurement data streamed from a site or asset (e.g. power, energy, status). Read via GET /telemetry/realtime.

chunks.title: Glossary: DER
chunks.text: DER (Technical): Distributed energy resources(e.g. battery, Photovoltaic)

chunks.title: Glossary: Dispatch
chunks.text: Dispatch (Technical): An instruction sent to an asset or portfolio to change its power profile (increase, reduce, shift) at a given time. Triggered via POST /dispatch/activate.

chunks.title: Glossary: Setpoint
chunks.text: Setpoint (Technical): A target operating value (e.g. a power level in kW) pushed to an asset so it adjusts its behaviour. Set via PUT /schedule/setpoint.

chunks.title: Glossary: Constraint
chunks.text: Constraint (Technical): A limit that bounds what an asset or the grid can do at a given moment (e.g. max import, voltage limits). Constraints are shared between operators and the platform.

chunks.title: Glossary: Settlement
chunks.text: Settlement (Technical): The reconciliation step that turns delivered flexibility into verified volumes and payments — who did what, when, and what they are owed.

chunks.title: Glossary: Forecasting
chunks.text: Forecasting (Technical): Predicting future consumption, generation, or flexibility potential of a site, used to plan dispatch and bid into markets.

chunks.title: Glossary: Baseline
chunks.text: Baseline (Technical): The expected consumption profile a site would have followed without any flexibility action. Flexibility delivered is measured as the gap between baseline and actual.

chunks.title: Glossary: aFRR (automatic Frequency Restoration Reserve)
chunks.text: aFRR (automatic Frequency Restoration Reserve) (Technical): A fast, automatically-activated grid balancing service that restores frequency after an imbalance. One of the flexibility products a site can provide.

chunks.title: Glossary: mFRR (manual Frequency Restoration Reserve)
chunks.text: mFRR (manual Frequency Restoration Reserve) (Technical): A grid balancing reserve activated manually by the system operator, typically slower than aFRR. Another flexibility product served via the platform.

chunks.title: Glossary: Curtailment
chunks.text: Curtailment (Technical): Deliberately reducing a site's consumption (or a generator's output) in response to a grid signal or price — a core flexibility action.

chunks.title: Glossary: Demand response
chunks.text: Demand response (Technical): Adjusting electricity consumption in response to grid needs or price signals, rather than changing supply. The umbrella behaviour FlexReady enables at scale.

chunks.title: Glossary: EMS (Energy Management System)
chunks.text: EMS (Energy Management System) (Technical): Software that monitors and controls energy use across a site. Often the system FlexReady integrates with to read data and apply setpoints.

chunks.title: Glossary: BMS (Building Management System)
chunks.text: BMS (Building Management System) (Technical): Software controlling a building's technical equipment (HVAC, lighting). A common source of site data and a control point for flexibility.

chunks.title: Glossary: EBO (EcoStruxure Building Operation)
chunks.text: EBO (EcoStruxure Building Operation) (Technical): Schneider Electric's building management platform. In pilots, the EMS/BMS feeding site data into FlexReady.

chunks.title: Glossary: IEC 62746-4
chunks.text: IEC 62746-4 (Technical): An international standard for the interface between grid operators and demand-side resources. The FlexReady northbound APIs align with it for interoperability.

chunks.title: Glossary: LOB (Line of Business)
chunks.text: LOB (Line of Business) (Technical): An internal Schneider business unit. FlexReady is the shared layer that lets every LOB deliver flexibility without rebuilding its own products.

chunks.title: Glossary: SLA (Service Level Agreement)
chunks.text: SLA (Service Level Agreement) (Technical): The committed levels of service (response times, severity handling, release notice) the platform guarantees during the Run phase.

chunks.title: Glossary: Flexibility
chunks.text: Flexibility (Commercial): The ability to shift, reduce, or increase electricity use or generation on demand. The core value FlexReady helps organizations monetize and grid operators rely on.

chunks.title: Glossary: Flexibility services
chunks.text: Flexibility services (Commercial): Market products built on flexibility (balancing, capacity, congestion relief) that organizations get paid to provide.

chunks.title: Glossary: Aggregator
chunks.text: Aggregator (Commercial): A company that pools flexibility from many sites and sells it on energy markets. A key commercial partner and a primary user of the FlexReady API.

chunks.title: Glossary: DSO (Distribution System Operator)
chunks.text: DSO (Distribution System Operator) (Commercial): The operator of the local electricity distribution grid. A core market actor that requests and consumes flexibility to manage congestion.

chunks.title: Glossary: Energy provider / supplier
chunks.text: Energy provider / supplier (Commercial): The company selling electricity to end customers. Reads tariff and settlement data from the platform.

chunks.title: Glossary: Energy Interactive Product
chunks.text: Energy Interactive Product (Commercial): Schneider's centralized integration layer that standardizes how internal systems interact with external flexibility actors. FlexReady is its API surface.

chunks.title: Glossary: Value proposition
chunks.text: Value proposition (Commercial): The core promise to the customer: deliver flexibility services without rebuilding core products, via one unified, standardized, secure layer.

chunks.title: Glossary: Exchange (Schneider Electric Exchange)
chunks.text: Exchange (Schneider Electric Exchange) (Commercial): The marketplace where the FlexReady API is published and where partners obtain access and subscription keys.

chunks.title: Glossary: Subscription key
chunks.text: Subscription key (Commercial): The credential a partner obtains on Exchange to access the FlexReady API under a given commercial plan.

chunks.title: Glossary: MVP (Minimum Viable Product)
chunks.text: MVP (Minimum Viable Product) (Commercial): The first usable version of the offer, used to validate value with early customers before scaling to enterprise-wide adoption.

chunks.title: Glossary: ARR (Annual Recurring Revenue)
chunks.text: ARR (Annual Recurring Revenue) (Commercial): The normalized yearly value of subscription revenue — a key metric for the business model's viability.

chunks.title: Glossary: Use case
chunks.text: Use case (Commercial): A concrete, named scenario showing how a customer derives value (e.g. SDEM50, IntenCity), used in promotion and proof of value.

chunks.title: Glossary: Onboarding
chunks.text: Onboarding (Commercial): The structured process of bringing a new site or partner live on the platform — configuration, skill-building, first results (detailed on the Onboarding page).

chunks.title: Glossary: Run phase
chunks.text: Run phase (Commercial): The operational life of the service after go-live: monitoring, support, incident handling and release management (detailed on the Run & SLA page).

chunks.title: Glossary: System Operator
chunks.text: System Operator (Persona): Operates the transmission grid and procures balancing services. Reads constraint and dispatch data to keep the grid stable.

chunks.title: Glossary: Network Operator
chunks.text: Network Operator (Persona): Manages a portion of the grid network; writes constraints and settlement data to the platform and consumes telemetry.

chunks.title: Glossary: Aggregator (persona)
chunks.text: Aggregator (persona) (Persona): Pools and dispatches flexibility across sites; writes settlement orders and dispatch to FlexReady and reads telemetry and forecasting.

chunks.title: Glossary: Asset Owner / Operator
chunks.text: Asset Owner / Operator (Persona): Owns or runs the physical sites and assets providing flexibility; reads constraints and telemetry, receives dispatch instructions.

chunks.title: Glossary: Energy Provider (persona)
chunks.text: Energy Provider (persona) (Persona): Supplies electricity to customers; reads tariff and settlement data from the platform.

chunks.title: Glossary: FlexReady Platform Operator
chunks.text: FlexReady Platform Operator (Persona): The central role operating the Energy Interactive platform itself — routing telemetry, dispatch, forecasting and settlement between all other roles.
